reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) — a key this population has never seen
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR DOES LESS, AND KNOWABLY SO. Ours mints an identity (a slot and an entry in the identity store — there is no per-index `links` cell, so a row carries nothing per index at all), copies the row, walks the copy's own names to refuse the ones a row may not carry, stamps the slot, stamps the collection and records the row on the presence channel so every index and every whole-population reader hears about it. The floor allocates one copy and hashes one string. Direction: this inflates our ratio, and no three-line floor can close the gap — what the extra buys is that anything subscribed to this population, or indexing it, is woken by this insert. The tracked row below is the closest a few lines get. Both sides abandon their container between passes and both are collected outside the clock, so the GC of what each allocated is NOT inside either number; our allocation per row is roughly three objects to the floor's one, and that debt is paid later.

reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) with the entity stored without a copy (oimInsertEntityWithoutCopy) — a key this population has never seen
reading.caveat: Neither side copies the row: both store the object they were handed, and both probe the key before filing it, as an upsert must. Ours still mints an identity, files it in the identity store, stamps it on the channel and runs the insert path of writeContentByKey; the floor hashes one string. A pass fills an empty world rebuilt outside the clock, and ours closes it with db.flush().
